passage:
The doctrine of promissory estoppel occupies an uneasy position within the common law of contracts. Classical contract doctrine holds that a promise is legally enforceable only when it is supported by consideration — that is, when the promisee has given something of value in exchange. Promissory estoppel departs from this requirement by rendering certain promises enforceable even in the absence of consideration, provided that the promisee has reasonably relied upon the promise to his or her detriment. The doctrine was first articulated in systematic form by American courts in the early twentieth century and was later codified in the Restatement (Second) of Contracts, adopted in the United States in 1979, which states that a promise is binding if it is one that the promisor should reasonably have expected to induce action or forbearance on the part of the promisee and which does in fact induce such action or forbearance.

Despite this codification, courts have applied promissory estoppel inconsistently, producing outcomes that are difficult to reconcile. Two strands of doctrine have emerged. Under the first — sometimes called the "reliance" strand — courts treat detrimental reliance as fully substituting for consideration, so that a plaintiff who establishes reasonable reliance may recover expectation damages equivalent to those available under a fully bargained contract. Under the second — the "equitable" strand — courts treat the doctrine as a limited remedy of conscience, awarding only reliance damages designed to restore the plaintiff to the position occupied before the promise was made, not the position that performance would have secured. A 1991 decision of the New Jersey Supreme Court illustrates the tension: the court awarded full expectation damages to an employee who had relocated across the country in reasonable reliance on a promise of long-term employment, while a contemporaneous decision of a California intermediate appellate court, presented with nearly identical facts, confined recovery to moving expenses alone. The New Jersey court grounded its holding in the principle that promissory estoppel should, wherever possible, approximate the remedies available in classical contract; the California court reasoned that the absence of a bargained exchange warranted a correspondingly restrained remedy.

The inconsistency in remedial outcomes reflects a deeper theoretical disagreement about the purpose of promissory estoppel. Those who favor the reliance strand argue that the doctrine exists to protect reasonable expectations generated by promises, and that restricting recovery to reliance damages systematically undercompensates plaintiffs and undermines the policy of holding promisors to their word. Those who favor the equitable strand counter that granting expectation damages in the absence of consideration blurs the distinction between contract and promissory estoppel and may deter socially useful promises by exposing promisors to liability disproportionate to any benefit received. Neither position is without force, and the case for a unified remedial rule has not yet been made convincingly. Regrettably, it seems unlikely that courts will converge on a single approach until a legislature or a supreme court of a major jurisdiction issues authoritative guidance — guidance that, one hopes, will take seriously both the reliance interests of promisees and the reasonable expectations of promisors who make informal promises in good faith.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Promissory estoppel was first codified in the 1979 Restatement (Second) of Contracts, which defines the conditions under which a promise lacking consideration may be enforceable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The doctrine of promissory estoppel has been applied inconsistently by courts, reflecting a deeper theoretical dispute about whether the doctrine's purpose is to protect reliance or to serve as a limited equitable remedy, and this inconsistency remains unresolved.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Courts should adopt a unified rule requiring that promissory estoppel plaintiffs receive full expectation damages whenever reasonable reliance on a promise is established.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The 1991 decisions of the New Jersey Supreme Court and the California Court of Appeal illustrate why promissory estoppel should be abolished in favor of classical contract doctrine.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Promissory estoppel is theoretically incompatible with classical contract law because it dispenses with the consideration requirement on which all enforceable promises depend.

explanations.correct: The passage traces the doctrine's codification, then devotes two paragraphs to explaining that courts apply it inconsistently (reliance vs. equitable strand) because of an unresolved theoretical disagreement about its purpose. B captures this full arc.
explanations.A: Too narrow — this describes only the first paragraph's historical background, not the passage's overall argument about inconsistency and its causes.
explanations.C: Overstates the author's position. The author says 'the case for a unified remedial rule has not yet been made convincingly' and does not advocate for expectation damages across the board.
explanations.D: Inverts the passage — the author does not argue for abolishing promissory estoppel; the cases illustrate tension within the doctrine.
explanations.E: The passage treats this as background, not the thesis. The author is focused on remedial inconsistency, not theoretical incompatibility per se.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the current state of promissory estoppel doctrine can best be described as which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enthusiastic endorsement of the equitable strand, whose cautious approach to damages preserves the distinction between contract and promissory estoppel

choices.label: B
choices.text: Strong approval of the reliance strand, since courts should wherever possible approximate classical contract remedies

choices.label: C
choices.text: Resigned acceptance that no single approach will ever be adopted and that the inconsistency is a permanent feature of the common law

choices.label: D
choices.text: Critical concern about persisting inconsistency combined with measured hope that authoritative guidance will eventually produce a balanced resolution

choices.label: E
choices.text: Confident satisfaction that the Restatement (Second) has already provided sufficient guidance to resolve the tension between the two strands

explanations.correct: The author says 'neither position is without force,' notes that the case for a unified rule 'has not yet been made convincingly,' expresses regret at the lack of convergence, and ends with 'one hopes' — signaling critical concern plus cautious optimism. D captures both the negative appraisal and the guarded hope.
explanations.A: Overstates the author's sympathy for one side. The author explicitly says 'neither position is without force.'
explanations.B: Same trap as A but in the other direction — the author does not endorse the reliance strand, only reports that its proponents favor expectation damages.
explanations.C: Too pessimistic. 'Resigned acceptance' contradicts the closing 'one hopes' and the call for authoritative guidance.
explanations.E: Directly contradicted by the passage, which says inconsistency persists despite codification.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and contrasted with an alternative doctrine; the two alternatives are illustrated by a historical case; and the passage concludes by endorsing one alternative.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legal doctrine is situated within classical contract theory; the doctrine's inconsistent judicial application is illustrated by contrasting decisions; and the underlying theoretical disagreement is identified and evaluated, with a call for authoritative resolution.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A problem in contract law is identified; a legislative solution is proposed and assessed; and the passage concludes that the solution is inadequate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A legal doctrine is defined; a single illustrative case is analyzed in depth; and the author concludes that the case was wrongly decided.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Competing theoretical positions on contract law are surveyed; the passage then traces their historical development in American courts; and a preferred theoretical framework is adopted.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 situates promissory estoppel within classical contract doctrine and notes its codification. Paragraph 2 presents the two judicial strands and illustrates them with contrasting 1991 decisions. Paragraph 3 identifies the theoretical disagreement driving the inconsistency and calls, with cautious hope, for authoritative guidance. B tracks this sequence accurately.
explanations.A: Mis-states the conclusion — the author does not endorse either alternative; also, the contrast is within promissory estoppel, not between it and an alternative doctrine.
explanations.C: No legislative solution is proposed; the passage instead calls for one and notes its absence.
explanations.D: Two cases are discussed, not one; the author does not conclude either was wrongly decided, though the New Jersey approach receives implicit approval.
explanations.E: The passage does not trace historical development in this order, and no preferred theoretical framework is adopted.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, which one of the following is true of the Restatement (Second) of Contracts?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It was drafted by the United States Congress and signed into law in 1979.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It requires courts to award expectation damages whenever promissory estoppel is established.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It defines a promise as binding when the promisor could reasonably have foreseen that it would induce action or forbearance by the promisee and when it does in fact induce such action or forbearance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It abolished the consideration requirement in all contracts governed by American common law.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It resolved the tension between the reliance and equitable strands of promissory estoppel by specifying the remedies available to successful plaintiffs.

explanations.correct: The passage states that the Restatement defines a promise as binding 'if it is one that the promisor should reasonably have expected to induce action or forbearance on the part of the promisee and which does in fact induce such action or forbearance.' C is a close paraphrase of this.
explanations.A: The Restatement is not a congressional statute; it was 'adopted' — a choice that omits the fact that Restatements are products of the American Law Institute, not Congress. The passage does not say Congress drafted it.
explanations.B: The passage says nothing about the Restatement specifying remedies; the remedial inconsistency arose despite the codification.
explanations.D: The passage says promissory estoppel 'departs from' the consideration requirement in specific circumstances; it does not abolish consideration generally.
explanations.E: Directly contradicted — the passage notes that inconsistency in remedial outcomes persists after codification.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that a court applying the equitable strand of promissory estoppel would hold which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A plaintiff who established reasonable reliance on an unfulfilled promise would be entitled to the full benefit of the bargain as though a contract had been formed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The absence of consideration in a promissory estoppel claim justifies limiting any recovery to the costs the plaintiff actually incurred in relying on the promise.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Promissory estoppel claims should be resolved by applying classical contract doctrine whenever the parties had equal bargaining power.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A court applying promissory estoppel should treat the doctrine identically to a fully bargained contract in order to deter promisors from breaking informal promises.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reliance damages are appropriate only when the plaintiff can also demonstrate that consideration was given at some earlier stage of the parties' relationship.

explanations.correct: The passage describes the equitable strand as one that 'treat[s] the doctrine as a limited remedy of conscience, awarding only reliance damages designed to restore the plaintiff to the position occupied before the promise was made.' This supports B — recovery is limited to actual costs incurred, because the absence of consideration warrants a restrained remedy.
explanations.A: This describes the reliance strand, not the equitable strand.
explanations.C: The passage makes no mention of bargaining power as a criterion under either strand.
explanations.D: This mirrors the reliance strand's aspiration to approximate classical contract remedies — the opposite of the equitable strand.
explanations.E: The passage does not connect the equitable strand to any requirement of prior consideration; indeed, promissory estoppel by definition operates without consideration.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of the 1991 New Jersey and California decisions serves primarily to:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Demonstrate that state courts in the United States are more willing than federal courts to award expectation damages in promissory estoppel cases.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Illustrate the concrete remedial divergence that results when courts apply competing strands of promissory estoppel doctrine to similar facts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Argue that the California court reached the correct result by limiting recovery to relocation expenses alone.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Provide historical evidence that promissory estoppel doctrine was first developed in New Jersey rather than in California.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Suggest that employment disputes are the most common context in which promissory estoppel claims arise.

explanations.correct: The two decisions appear immediately after the passage introduces the reliance and equitable strands, and they instantiate those strands in nearly identical factual circumstances — one awarding full expectation damages, the other confining recovery to moving expenses. Their function is to make the abstract doctrinal divergence concrete and visible. B captures this illustrative purpose.
explanations.A: The cases both involve state courts; no comparison to federal courts is made.
explanations.C: The author does not endorse the California outcome; the passage implies sympathy for the New Jersey approach by contextualizing it within the broader reliance-protection rationale.
explanations.D: The passage says promissory estoppel was first articulated systematically by 'American courts in the early twentieth century,' not in New Jersey specifically, and the cases are from 1991.
explanations.E: The passage does not generalize about which contexts produce the most promissory estoppel claims.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the argument made by proponents of the equitable strand of promissory estoppel?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Empirical studies show that restricting promissory estoppel recovery to reliance damages causes promisors to make fewer informal promises that later induce significant reliance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Many jurisdictions that award full expectation damages in promissory estoppel cases also report high rates of commercial litigation involving formal contracts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Legal scholars have argued that the consideration requirement was not part of the original common law of England.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Courts in jurisdictions that award only reliance damages in promissory estoppel cases frequently encounter difficulty calculating the precise amount of those damages.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A survey of promissory estoppel plaintiffs found that a majority had sustained losses far exceeding the costs they incurred in reliance, because they had foregone other opportunities in reasonable expectation of the promised performance.

explanations.correct: The equitable strand restricts recovery to reliance damages on the grounds that this restores the plaintiff to the pre-promise position and avoids exposing promisors to disproportionate liability. If plaintiffs' actual losses routinely exceed reliance costs because of foregone opportunities — losses that only expectation damages would cover — then restricting recovery to reliance damages systematically undercompensates promisees, directly undermining the equitable strand's claim to be an adequate and fair remedy.
explanations.A: This would actually support the equitable strand's concern about deterring informal promises — it suggests that limiting liability does affect promisor behavior, but in a way that reduces beneficial promises, which cuts against both strands. The effect on the equitable strand's core argument (that reliance damages are the right measure) is unclear, making A weaker than E.
explanations.B: Irrelevant to the equitable strand's rationale. High litigation rates in expectation-damages jurisdictions might weakly support concerns about overexposure, but the connection is too attenuated.
explanations.C: This concerns the historical origins of the consideration requirement, not the merits of the equitable vs. reliance remedial debate.
explanations.D: This is a practical difficulty for courts applying the equitable strand, but it does not undermine the substantive argument that reliance damages are the appropriate measure; it is at most a procedural complication.
